title: The Credit-Report Error Has Two Addresses
subtitle: Correcting a mistake usually means contacting both the reporting company and the business that supplied the information. Here’s how to make the process clear, documented and easier to follow.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table, comparing a credit report with a folder of account records and a notebook.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light kitchen-table scene: two friends review a printed credit report beside a laptop, a few neatly organized account documents and a notebook with dates and follow-up steps. The person whose report it is leads the review; the other listens and helps keep track.
body: A mistake can travel through two systems

A credit-report error can feel like one problem with one obvious fix. In practice, the information has at least two addresses: the credit reporting company that assembled the report and the lender, collector or other business that supplied the entry. They have different roles, so a dispute sent to only one may leave an important part of the process untouched.

A reporting company investigates a dispute and generally sends it, along with relevant information you provide, to the business that furnished the data. That business checks its own records and reports back. For account information, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau recommends contacting both the reporting company and the furnisher. The Federal Trade Commission also advises disputing with each reporting company whose report contains the error, then contacting the business that supplied it. [1] [2]

That two-address approach is the useful starting point—not a promise that every disputed item will be removed. The goal is to correct information that is inaccurate or incomplete, or that cannot be verified. An accurate negative entry is not made inaccurate simply because it is frustrating or affects a credit application.
First, identify the entry and the specific problem

Get a current copy of the report and locate the exact item. Note which reporting company’s report it appears on: information can differ among reports, so an entry may need attention with more than one company. Check the details that can be wrong, such as the account owner, balance, payment status, dates, or whether an account belongs to you. The FTC says consumers should check whether their reports are accurate and complete, and notes that identity theft can lead to accounts opened in a person’s name appearing on a report as unpaid or delinquent. [2]

Then state what you believe is wrong and why. “This account is not mine” is a clear basis if true. So is “I paid this balance on this date, but the report shows it unpaid,” when you have records supporting that claim. By contrast, “Please remove this because it is hurting my score” does not identify inaccurate information.

Be precise without trying to write like a lawyer. Identify the account by the information shown on the report, describe the specific detail you dispute, and say what you believe the correct information should be. If you are unsure, separate what you know from what you want investigated. Accuracy is more useful than forceful language.
Send the dispute to both relevant parties

Use the reporting company’s official dispute process, and follow its instructions for submitting documents. If you write, include enough information to identify yourself and the report entry, explain the issue, and clearly request an investigation. For an account entry, also send a dispute to the business that supplied it, using that business’s stated dispute channel. Keep the two submissions consistent, but address each to the right organization. [1]

A practical example: suppose a report shows a balance on a card you closed and paid. You could dispute the balance with each reporting company showing it, and contact the card issuer with the account details and proof of payment. The reporting company can investigate through the furnisher; contacting the issuer directly gives the source of the information a separate opportunity to check its records.

If an entry appears to involve identity theft, don’t assume an ordinary account dispute is the only step you need. Use the official identity-theft reporting and account-protection processes that apply to your situation as well. And if someone is helping you— a partner, relative or trusted friend—the person whose report it is should choose what to share and remain in control of submissions and account details.
Build a small, useful evidence file

A dispute is easier to track when its evidence is collected before you submit it. Make a short record with five parts: the report entry, the reason it appears wrong, the documents that support your account, where you sent the dispute, and the date it went out. Add a copy of each letter or online submission and any confirmation number.

Send copies, not original documents. Depending on the issue, relevant records might include a payment confirmation, account statement, letter confirming closure, identity document requested by the reporting company, or correspondence from the business. Include only material that helps explain the particular error; a large pile of unrelated paperwork can obscure the point. CFPB guidance recommends describing the disputed information, explaining the basis, providing supporting copies and keeping copies of what you send. [1]

For mailed disputes, use the address designated for disputes rather than assuming a payment address or general customer-service address is appropriate. For online submissions, save or print the confirmation and the information you entered. If you submit through more than one channel, note what went where. A simple paper folder or private digital file is enough; the goal is a reliable record, not a complicated case-management system.
Know the clock—and what can change it

A reporting company generally has 30 days to investigate a dispute. In some circumstances, the period can extend to 45 days, including when relevant information is submitted during the initial investigation period. CFPB guidance also describes a 45-day period for certain disputes filed after a free annual report. Once the investigation is complete, results generally must be sent within five business days. [3]

These are general federal timelines, not a reason to assume that a particular investigation will finish on a specific day. Write down the submission date and use it to track the response. If you send additional information after filing, record when and how you sent it; it may matter to the timeline. Watch for requests for additional identifying information and respond through the official channel if needed.

If the expected response does not arrive, check the status with the reporting company or furnisher using the contact details from its official materials. Keep a note of the date, the channel used and any next step promised. A calm, dated record is more useful than relying on memory or sending the same explanation repeatedly without knowing whether it was received.
Read the result, then decide what remains

When the investigation ends, compare the result with the original entry and the records you submitted. If information is found inaccurate or incomplete, it should be corrected; information that cannot be verified may be removed, as appropriate. But filing a dispute alone does not guarantee a particular outcome. Federal law also provides a route to add a brief statement to a file when a dispute remains unresolved. [1]

If you disagree with the result, identify exactly what is still wrong and what evidence may not have been considered. You can contact the reporting company and the furnisher again with that focused explanation, and check the relevant report afterward to see whether the change appears. Keep the first result letter with your original record so the next communication can refer to the investigation already completed.

If the disputed information is accurate, a dispute is not a way to erase it. The FTC distinguishes inaccurate information from accurate negative information, which generally cannot be removed just because it has an adverse effect. [2] Be cautious of anyone promising to remove accurate history or guarantee a score increase in exchange for a fee. The useful question is not whether an entry is unwelcome, but whether it is wrong, incomplete or unverifiable.
A five-line record that keeps the process manageable

Before you close the folder, make sure you can answer five questions: What exact entry is disputed? What is the specific reason? What evidence was sent, and were the originals kept? Which reporting company and furnisher were contacted, and on what dates? What response arrived, and what—if anything—needs follow-up?

That small record helps whether you handle the process alone or ask someone you trust to help organize documents. If another person assists, agree what they may see and do; don’t share passwords or give up control of your report just to make the paperwork easier. For a U.S. consumer, this article describes the general federal dispute process, not personalized legal advice. State protections may add rights or procedures, and a complicated identity, mixed-file or unresolved case may call for more tailored help.

The central idea is straightforward: make the error specific, put the dispute in front of the organizations responsible for it, and keep a clear account of what happened next. That turns a stressful, vague task into a sequence you can verify and manage.
